title: Convex Sets And Cones
notes: Open the section as a shift from seeing convexity as a picture to treating it as a certificate. The lecture will use the printed span only for terminology and orientation, then build synthetic tests: segment containment, convex weights, conic weights, halfspace inspections, and explicit failures.

title: Segment Test
notes: Make the segment test feel like the smallest possible convexity experiment. Pick two displayed points first, then sweep the parameter t. The important habit is that a convexity claim is not just a shaded region; it commits to every intermediate point between every admissible pair.

title: Convex Combinations
notes: Introduce convex combinations as the algebra behind the segment sweep. The weights carry all the geometry: nonnegative prevents extrapolation, and sum one keeps the point affine rather than conic. Ask students to read the formula as a certificate that can be checked line by line.

title: Convex Hull As Closure Under Mixing
notes: Use the hull picture to turn repeated mixing into an object. Start with a finite point cloud, allow every convex combination, and the filled polygon appears as the closure of all possible averages. The displayed weights are not decorative; they are a membership certificate for the interior point.

title: Caratheodory-Style Compression View
notes: Frame the Caratheodory-style slide as compression, not as a mysterious theorem. In the plane, an interior point may be written with many positive weights, but redundant support can be removed until only three points remain. The JSON artifact records one concrete before and after certificate.

title: Cones And Positive Scaling
notes: Cones add a second closure rule: once a point is admitted, every positive scaling of it is admitted as well. Emphasize that this removes the normalization sum one. The origin becomes an anchor, rays become primitive evidence, and addition of admissible rays supplies the fan.

title: Conic Combinations
notes: Conic combinations are the cone analogue of convex combinations. The check is simpler and harsher: coefficients must be nonnegative, but they do not have to sum to one. Read the target point as generated evidence, then mention that a negative coefficient would point outside the cone certificate.

title: Pointed, Flat, And Full-Dimensional Examples
notes: Use the taxonomy slide to separate three issues that are often blurred. A flat cone can be low-dimensional, a pointed cone can have no line through the origin, and a full-dimensional cone can still be sharply constrained. These examples prepare students for rank and lineality checks.

title: Polyhedral Cones From Generators
notes: Treat a polyhedral cone as the result of finitely many generator rays. The fan is a computational object: build the matrix of generators, solve for nonnegative coefficients, then inspect rank to decide the dimension of the span. Extreme rays are the irreducible visual edges of the fan.

title: Dual Inspection By Halfspaces
notes: Dual inspection reverses the direction of evidence. Instead of producing the point from generators, choose a linear functional and check its sign on every generator. If all generator tests are nonnegative, the functional is in the dual cone; one failed dot product is a separating diagnostic.

title: Convexity Under Intersection
notes: Intersection is the quiet workhorse operation. Each convex set promises to keep the whole segment between two shared points, so the segment stays in every member at once and therefore in the intersection. This explains why halfspace descriptions are so powerful for polyhedra and cones.

title: Nonconvex Failure Gallery
notes: The failure gallery is meant to sharpen the eye. Each mini-example gives endpoints that pass local membership but a midpoint or chord that leaves the set. Ask the room to name the failing witness before reading the caption; a single witness is enough to disprove convexity.

title: Numerical Membership Tests
notes: Translate the geometry into numerical tests without pretending the tests prove infinite cases by sampling alone. The algorithmic checks are certificates when they solve equations with sign constraints, and they are counterexamples when they find explicit violating points. Residuals tell us whether the computation matches the mathematical claim.

title: Recap / Inspection Prompt
notes: Close by returning to the inspection prompt. For any proposed set or cone, students should ask for the relevant certificate first: segment containment, convex weights, conic weights, halfspace signs, or a counterexample. The section becomes a toolkit for later separation, support, and duality arguments.
